entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen14953" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14954" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14955" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14955" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14954" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14956" type="x-p"/> Artaxerxes, observing the sorrow of Nehemiah, inquires into the cause, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.1">Neh 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.2">Neh 2:2</reference>. Nehemiah shows him the cause, and requests permission to go and rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.3-Neh.2.6">Neh 2:3-6</reference>. The king grants it, and gives him letters to the governors beyond the river, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.7">Neh 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.8">Neh 2:8</reference>. He sets out on his journey, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.9">Neh 2:9</reference>. Sanballat and Tobiah are grieved to find he had got such a commission, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.10">Neh 2:10</reference>. He comes to Jerusalem; and, without informing any person of his business, examines by night the state of the city, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.11-Neh.2.16">Neh 2:11-16</reference>. He informs the priests, nobles, and rulers, of his design and commission, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.17">Neh 2:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.18">Neh 2:18</reference>. The design is turned into contempt by Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.19">Neh 2:19</reference>. Nehemiah gives them a suitable answer, Neh 2:20 . Verse 1 Month Nisan - Answering to a part of our March and April. Aelian, Hist. Var. lib. i. c. 32, uses the same form of speech in reference to Artaxerxes Mnemon, one of the Persian kings, Βασιλευ Αρταξερξη, δι' αιωνος βασιλευοις, "O King Artaxerxes, may you reign for ever," when speaking of the custom of presenting them annually with an offering of earth and water; as if they had said, May you reign for ever over these!

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen14962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14963" type="x-p"/> The city of my fathers' sepulchres - The tombs of the dead were sacred among the ancients, and nothing could appear to them more detestable than disturbing the ashes or remains of the dead. Nehemiah knew that in mentioning this circumstance he should strongly interest the feelings of the Persian king.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen14963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14964" type="x-p"/> The queen also sitting by him - Who probably forwarded his suit. This was not Esther, as Dean Prideaux supposes, nor perhaps the same Artaxerxes who had taken her to be queen; nor does שגל shegal signify queen, but rather harlot or concubine, she who was chief favourite. The Septuagint translate it παλλακη, harlot; and properly too. See the introduction. <div eID="gen14964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14965" type="x-p"/> I set him a time - How long this time was we are not told; it is by no means likely that it was long, probably no more than six months or a year; after which he either returned, or had his leave of absence lengthened; for in the same year we find he was made governor of the Jews, in which office he continued twelve years, viz., from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, <reference osisRef="Neh.5.14">Neh 5:14</reference>. He then returned to Susa; and after staying a short time, had leave to return to rectify some abuses that Tobiah the Ammonite had introduced into the temple, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.6">Neh 13:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.7">Neh 13:7</reference>, and several others of which the people themselves were guilty. After having performed this service, it is likely he returned to the Persian king, and died in his office of cup-bearer; but of this latter circumstance we have no mention in the text.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen14965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14966" type="x-p"/> Asaph the keeper of the king's forest - הפרדס hapardes of the paradise of the king. This I believe is originally a Persian word; it frequently occurs in Arabic, ferdoos, and in Greek, παραδεισος, and in both signifies a pleasant garden, vineyard, pleasure garden, and what we call a paradise. <div eID="gen14966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14967" type="x-p"/> Above the hall of audience, in the imperial palace at Dehli, the following Persian couplet is inscribed: - "If there be a paradise on the face of the earth, this is it, this is it, this is it." <div eID="gen14967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14968" type="x-p"/> Thus we find that the word is applied to denote splendid apartments, as well as fine gardens; in a word, any place of pleasure and delight. The king's forest mentioned in the text might have been the same to Artaxerxes, as the New Forest was to William the Conqueror, or Windsor Forest to the late amiable sovereign of the British people, George the Third. <div eID="gen14968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14969" type="x-p"/> And the king granted me, etc. - This noble spirited man attributes every thing to God. He might have said, I had been long a faithful servant to the king; and he was disposed, in reward of my fidelity, to grant my request; but he would not say so: "He granted my request, because the good hand of my God was upon me." God favored me, and influenced the king's heart to do what I desired.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen14969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14970" type="x-p"/> Sanballat the Horonite - Probably a native of Horonaim, a Moabite by birth, and at this time governor of the Samaritans under the king of Persia. <div eID="gen14970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14971" type="x-p"/> Tobiah the servant - He was an Ammonite; and here, under the Persian king, joint governor with Sanballat. Some suppose that the Sanballat here mentioned was the same who persuaded Alexander to build a temple on Mount Gerizim in favor of the Samaritans. Pelagius thinks there were two governors of this name.
